questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis with a clean base and raised, rolled edges. Regional inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate is the investigation of choice. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: The painless, indurated ulcer with non-tender lymphadenopathy is classic primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum). Dark-field microscopy identifies the spirochete. Chancroid causes painful ulcers with tender nodes. LGV causes groove sign lymphadenopathy. Donovanosis lacks significant lymphadenopathy.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops a photosensitive butterfly rash. Which immunofluorescence finding at the dermoepidermal junction is most specific for SLE?
opts: IgG and C3 deposits in lesional skin only
IgG and C3 deposits in both lesional and non-lesional skin
IgA deposits in a linear pattern
C3 deposits alone in papillary dermis
questions.exp: The lupus band test showing IgG and C3 deposits at the DEJ in both lesional AND non-lesional skin is characteristic of SLE, differentiating it from subacute cutaneous lupus (lesional skin only). Linear IgA is for linear IgA disease. C3 alone in papillary dermis suggests dermatitis herpetiformis-like.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic patient presents with painful swelling of the right foot with multiple discharging sinuses. Microscopy of the grain from the discharge shows broad septate hyphae with chlamydospores. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Madurella mycetomatis is the most common cause of eumycetoma in India, producing black grains on microscopy with broad septate hyphae and chlamydospores. Nocardia and Actinomadura cause actinomycetoma (bacterial) with different grain types. Fusarium is less common and usually causes lighter-colored grains.

questions.q: A 30-year-old presents with multiple hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation. Slit-skin smear is negative. Histopathology shows granuloma formation around dermal nerves with Langhans giant cells. What type of leprosy is this?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas around and within dermal nerve sheaths with Langhans giant cells, and a negative smear (paucibacillary). BT also shows granulomas but they are less well-formed. LL shows foamy macrophages (lepra cells) with many bacilli. Indeterminate shows non-specific infiltrate.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the shaft of the penis, along with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy and fever. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the first-line treatment?
opts: Acyclovir 200mg five times daily for 10 days
Acyclovir 400mg three times daily for 7-10 days
questions.exp: For primary genital herpes (HSV-2), oral acyclovir 400mg TDS for 7-10 days is standard first-line therapy. Valacyclovir 1g BD for 10 days is an alternative with better bioavailability. Famciclovir 250mg TDS is also used. The Tzanck smear with multinucleated giant cells confirms herpes but does not distinguish HSV types.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a non-healing ulcer on the lower lip of 3 months duration. Biopsy shows islands of malignant squamous cells with horn pearls and moderate stromal reaction. Which lymph node group is involved first in metastasis?
questions.exp: The lower lip drains primarily to the submental and submandibular lymph nodes as first-echelon nodes. The upper lip drains to parotid and submandibular nodes. Posterior auricular nodes drain the scalp. This SCC of lower lip has good prognosis when caught early.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with intensely pruritic, tense bullae on the trunk and flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. ELISA is positive for anti-BP180 antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae, intense pruritus, and DIF showing linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Anti-BP180 (type XVII collagen) and anti-BP230 antibodies are hallmarks. Pemphigus shows intraepidermal split with intercellular IgG. DH shows granular IgA in papillary dermis. EBA also shows linear BMZ but targets type VII collagen.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male on prolonged dapsone therapy develops pallor and dyspnea. His methemoglobin level is 20%. Which enzyme deficiency makes patients more susceptible to dapsone-induced methemoglobinemia?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes methemoglobinemia via its hydroxylamine metabolite. Cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH methemoglobin reductase) deficiency predisposes to methemoglobinemia. G6PD deficiency predisposes to hemolytic anemia with dapsone. Treatment for methemoglobinemia is methylene blue. G6PD screening before dapsone is recommended.

questions.q: A 32-year-old presents with a tender erythematous nodule on the shin that shows histopathology of lobular panniculitis without vasculitis. She is on oral contraceptive pills. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum shows septal panniculitis (not lobular) classically, but OCP is a known trigger. However, the described lobular panniculitis without vasculitis in a woman on OCP most likely represents erythema nodosum in a broader clinical context. Erythema induratum (Bazin disease) shows lobular panniculitis WITH vasculitis and is TB-associated. Nodular vasculitis shows lobular panniculitis with vasculitis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old farmer presents with verrucous, warty plaques on the leg with occasional black dots. KOH mount shows 'medlar bodies' (sclerotic bodies). What is this condition?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is characterized by verrucous/cauliflower-like plaques on exposed areas and pathognomonic Medlar bodies (sclerotic cells/copper penny bodies) in tissue. Common agents: Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Cladosporium carrionii. Sporotrichosis shows asteroid bodies. Phaeohyphomycosis shows hyphae in tissue. Lobomycosis shows chain-like yeast cells.

questions.q: A neonate develops blistering within 24 hours of birth. Nikolsky sign is positive. Staphylococcus aureus is isolated from blood culture. Histopathology shows subcorneal cleavage. Which toxin is responsible?
questions.exp: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (serine proteases) produced by phage group II S. aureus. They cleave desmoglein 1 in the granular layer causing subcorneal blistering. TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome. Leukocidin destroys leukocytes. Protein A inhibits opsonization.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80) presents with multiple flesh-colored, umbilicated papules on the face and trunk. The causative virus belongs to which family?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of Poxviridae family. It is a DNA virus. In immunocompetent individuals, it is self-limiting, but in HIV patients with low CD4 counts, it can be extensive and recalcitrant. The pathognomonic finding is molluscum bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) on histology.

questions.q: A patient undergoing dermoscopy for a pigmented lesion shows an irregular pigment network, multiple regression areas, and atypical dotted vessels. Which dermoscopic criterion is most specific for melanoma?
questions.exp: Blue-white veil (a blue-white haze overlying a raised area) is the most specific dermoscopic criterion for melanoma. Atypical pigment network and irregular dots/globules are also suspicious but less specific. Regression structures (white scar-like areas) indicate melanoma regression but can occur in other lesions.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with Raynaud phenomenon, puffy fingers, and dysphagia. Her ANA is positive with nucleolar pattern. Anti-Scl-70 antibody is detected. What complication should be monitored most closely?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and predict interstitial lung disease (ILD) as the major complication. Anti-centromere antibodies predict pulmonary hypertension. Renal crisis (scleroderma renal crisis) is associated with diffuse SSc but specifically correlates with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with painful grouped vesicles along T5 dermatome, burning pain preceding rash by 3 days. Tzanck smear is positive. What is the most feared complication in elderly immunocompetent patients?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common and feared complication of herpes zoster, especially in elderly patients (>60 years). It is defined as pain persisting >3 months after rash resolution. Risk factors include advanced age, severity of acute pain, and ophthalmic involvement. Antiviral treatment within 72 hours reduces PHN risk.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with ring-shaped, itchy, scaly patches on the scalp with broken hair stubs and cervical lymphadenopathy. Wood's lamp examination shows bright green fluorescence. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes ectothrix tinea capitis with bright green fluorescence under Wood's lamp (due to pteridine). T. tonsurans causes endothrix infection with black dot ringworm and NO fluorescence. T. violaceum also causes endothrix without fluorescence. M. gypseum is geophilic and causes rare scalp infection.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male on methotrexate for psoriasis develops oral ulcers, cytopenias, and hair loss after a dose increase. What is the mechanism of methotrexate toxicity?
opts: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase causing folate depletion
Purine synthesis inhibition via AICAR accumulation
questions.exp: Methotrexate competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. This depletes reduced folate pools needed for purine and thymidine synthesis, affecting rapidly proliferating cells. AICAR accumulation also occurs but the primary mechanism is DHFR inhibition. Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue bypasses DHFR to counteract toxicity.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-crusted lesions on the face. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Which toxin from this organism can trigger acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.exp: In impetigo caused by nephritogenic strains of Group A Streptococcus, M protein (especially types 49, 55, 57) acts as antigen triggering immune complex deposition in glomeruli causing APSGN. Streptolysin O is detected by ASO titer (elevated in pharyngeal but NOT skin infection typically). Erythrogenic toxin causes scarlet fever. Hyaluronidase aids tissue spread.

questions.q: A patient with moderate plaque psoriasis achieves PASI 75 at week 12 with biological therapy. He develops recurrent RTI. The biologic works by blocking the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23. Which drug is this?
questions.exp: Ustekinumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23, blocking Th1 and Th17 pathways. Secukinumab and ixekizumab target IL-17A. Guselkumab targets the p19 subunit of IL-23 only. RTIs are a class effect of biologics due to immunosuppression.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with painless ulcerating papules on the inguinal region. Donovan bodies are seen on Giemsa stain of the tissue smear, appearing as 'safety pin' intracytoplasmic inclusions in mononuclear cells. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis is treated with doxycycline 100mg BD for at least 21 days (until complete healing). Azithromycin 1g weekly is an alternative. Ceftriaxone is used for gonorrhea and chancroid. Benzathine penicillin is used for syphilis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male with type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) presents with acute neuritis of ulnar nerve. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.exp: Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction occurring in borderline leprosy. Acute neuritis is a medical emergency requiring immediate systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 40-60mg/day) to prevent permanent nerve damage. Thalidomide is used for type 2 reaction (ENL) but is contraindicated in females of childbearing age. Anti-leprosy drugs should be continued.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with a 'stuck-on' appearance verrucous lesion on the trunk. Dermoscopy shows multiple milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Seborrheic keratosis has a classic 'stuck-on' appearance clinically and dermoscopy shows pathognomonic milia-like cysts (white round structures), comedo-like openings, and crypts (fissures and ridges). Melanocytic nevi show network, globules, or homogeneous pattern. Warts show dotted vessels in a mosaic pattern. Solar lentigo shows a moth-eaten border pattern.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male heavy smoker presents with a solitary ulcerated nodule on the lower lip for 4 months. Biopsy shows moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most important prognostic factor?
opts: Depth of invasion and perineural invasion
questions.exp: For cutaneous SCC and lip SCC, the most important prognostic factors are depth of invasion (Breslow thickness equivalent) and perineural invasion, which significantly increases risk of recurrence, metastasis, and mortality. The 2022 AJCC staging incorporates these features. Tumor size matters but depth and perineural invasion are more prognostically significant.

questions.q: During a punch biopsy of a suspected psoriasis plaque on the leg, the bleeding is controlled. What is the minimum width punch typically used to ensure adequate tissue for histopathological diagnosis in inflammatory dermatoses?
questions.exp: A 4mm punch biopsy is the minimum standard recommended for inflammatory dermatoses to provide adequate tissue for histopathological examination, including assessment of the epidermis, dermis, and sometimes superficial subcutis. 3mm may be used for thin skin areas. 6mm is used when more tissue is needed (e.g., panniculitis, where deep tissue is required).

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops a butterfly-shaped malar rash after sun exposure, along with oral ulcers and arthralgia. ANA is 1:640 with homogeneous pattern. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are positive. What HLA type is most strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Systemic lupus erythematosus is most strongly associated with HLA-DR2 (HLA-DRB1*1501) and HLA-DR3 (HLA-DRB1*0301). HLA-B27 is associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies. HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and pemphigus vulgaris. HLA-Cw6 is associated with psoriasis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with moist, cauliflower-like growths around the anal region. He has multiple sexual partners. PCR for HPV is positive. Which HPV types are most commonly responsible for condyloma acuminata?
questions.exp: Condyloma acuminata (anogenital warts) are caused predominantly by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, which rarely cause malignancy. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types causing cervical and anogenital carcinoma. HPV 31 and 33 are other high-risk types. HPV 2 and 4 cause common warts (verruca vulgaris).

questions.q: A patient with bullous pemphigoid on high-dose prednisolone is being considered for steroid-sparing therapy. Which agent works by inhibiting phospholipase A2 and is used as a first-line steroid-sparing agent in bullous pemphigoid?
questions.exp: Dapsone inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis and is thought to inhibit phospholipase A2 and the myeloperoxidase-H2O2-halide cytotoxic system. It is an effective steroid-sparing agent in bullous pemphigoid given the role of neutrophils and eosinophils in blister formation. Azathioprine and MMF are also used but work by different mechanisms (antimetabolites).

questions.q: A 55-year-old presents with palpable purpura on bilateral lower limbs with renal involvement and neuropathy. Skin biopsy shows leucocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on DIF. Serum cryoglobulins are detected. What is the likely trigger?
questions.exp: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (mixed cryoglobulinemia type II or III) with LCV on biopsy, renal and nerve involvement is most commonly triggered by hepatitis C virus infection (>90% of cases). HCV stimulates B-cell proliferation producing mixed cryoglobulins (IgM rheumatoid factor + polyclonal IgG). HSP shows IgA deposits but is typically in children without cryoglobulins.

questions.q: A 28-year-old fair-skinned woman develops erythema and burning on sun-exposed areas after starting a new medication for UTI. Phototesting shows decreased minimal erythema dose in UVA range. What drug is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) are among the most common causes of phototoxic reactions, predominantly mediated by UVA radiation. The reaction is dose-dependent and occurs on first exposure (unlike photoallergy which requires sensitization). Co-trimoxazole can cause both phototoxic and photoallergic reactions but is less common than fluoroquinolones for UTI.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with chronic relapsing vesicular eczema of the palms with intense pruritus. Patch testing is negative. There is seasonal worsening in summer. Which condition does this most likely represent?
questions.exp: Pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema) presents with intensely pruritic, deep-seated vesicles on the palms and lateral fingers with seasonal exacerbations in spring/summer. Patch testing is negative distinguishing it from ACD. It is associated with hyperhidrosis, emotional stress, and occasionally nickel sensitivity. KOH negative rules out tinea. Psoriasis shows scaling plaques without vesicles typically.
